questions.q: In the Meridian Logistics case study, what specific detail about the billing batch job's failures points to parent (account) skew as the cause?
options: The failures happen at random across all accounts with no pattern
The failures are consistently concentrated on the same handful of large national accounts
The failures only happen on records created in the last 24 hours
The failures only happen when the Status__c field is blank
questions.explain: Lock-related failures consistently tied to the same handful of large accounts is the signature of parent skew — those accounts have accumulated a disproportionate share of child Shipment__c records, creating lock contention during concurrent updates.

questions.q: What is the recommended first step for the billing batch job's lock failures, before considering serial mode?
options: Immediately requesting a custom index on AccountId
Deleting all Shipment__c records for the affected accounts
Disabling the role hierarchy entirely
Reorganizing the job's batches to group records by AccountId
questions.explain: Per Lesson 9's guidance, reorganizing batches to group by parent ID is the first fix to try for lock contention caused by skew, before escalating to serial mode.

questions.q: Why is the slow role reorganization (Symptom 3) specifically a sharing-recalculation problem rather than a record-locking problem like Symptom 2?
options: Because role moves never interact with sharing at all
Because Symptom 3 is actually identical to Symptom 2 and has the same root cause
Because every individual role move is triggering a full sharing recalculation against millions of Shipment__c records, one move at a time, rather than contention over a single parent's lock
Because role reorganizations always fail outright and never complete
questions.explain: Symptom 3's slowness comes from the cost of sharing recalculation scaling with data volume and being triggered repeatedly, once per role move — a different mechanism than the lock contention behind Symptom 2, even though both are write-path problems.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that fixing all three immediate symptoms without addressing the lack of any archiving process is incomplete?
options: Because years of closed-out, never-archived Shipment__c records keep padding the active working set that every other fix is fighting against, so the same problems would resurface worse as volume keeps growing
Because archiving is legally required by Salesforce's terms of service
Because Big Objects cannot be created unless archiving has already occurred
Because the billing job can only run against archived data
questions.explain: Without archiving, the active data set keeps growing, which makes query selectivity worse, skew worse, and sharing recalculation more expensive over time — fixing the three symptoms without addressing this means the same problems reappear, worse, later.

questions.q: In the recommended sequenced remediation plan, what is the first step, and why?
options: Immediately switch the billing job to serial mode, since that's the fastest fix

Establish an archiving process for closed-out Shipment__c records, since shrinking the active working set makes every other fix more effective and should happen before re-evaluating the other symptoms
Request a new Big Object with no further analysis
Delete the entire Shipment__c object and rebuild it from scratch
questions.explain: The plan sequences archiving first because it shrinks the active data set that every other fix (batch reorganization, custom index/skinny table evaluation, deferred sharing calculation) is working against — tackling it first makes the later fixes more effective and sometimes unnecessary at the same scale.
